title: The Elegant Flirt 6
content:
Half-expecting the old fuddy-duddy and the young fuddy-duddy to stage a midnight raid and drag him out of bed for a flogging, Wei Wuxian slept the whole night clutching his sword to his chest. Against all odds, the night passed in blessed, uninterrupted peace. By next morning, Nie Huaisang came bursting into his quarters, beaming ear-to-ear. "Brother Wei, the gods must be watching over you! The old man took off for Qinghe last night for the Discussion Conference at my family's estate. We're off the hook for days!"

With the old fossil out of the picture, handling the younger one would be child's play. Wei Wuxian scrambled out of bed, grinning from ear to ear as he tugged on his boots. "The stars have aligned! Heaven is smiling upon me!"

Beside him, Jiang Cheng was meticulously wiping down his blade, immediately raining on his parade. "Enjoy it while it lasts. The moment he's back, you're still getting skinned alive."

Wei Wuxian waved him off. "Why sweat over tomorrow when you're alive today? A day of freedom is a day won. Come on, I refuse to believe the Lan mountain doesn't have a few plump pheasants hiding in the woods."

Shoulder to shoulder, the trio made their way past the Elegant Room, the Cloud Recesses' main reception hall. Wei Wuxian pulled up short, eyes widening. "Wait, two little fuddy... Lan Zhan!"

A small retinue had just stepped out of the hall. The two youths leading the pack were carved from the same breathtaking jade, dressed in identical snow-white robes, their sword tassels and forehead ribbons trailing in the mountain breeze. The only divide was their aura. Wei Wuxian spotted the difference immediately: the one with the sour scowl was Lan Wangji, which meant the warm, serene one beside him had to be the other half of the Twin Jades of Lan, Ze-wu-jun Lan Xichen.

The moment Lan Wangji clocked Wei Wuxian, his brow pinched tight. He shot him a downright venomous glare—looking as if a single second longer in his presence would soil his soul—before snapping his gaze toward the far horizon.

Lan Xichen, however, offered a genial smile. "And who might these young gentlemen be?"

Jiang Cheng dropped into a crisp salute. "Jiang Wanyin of Yunmeng."

Wei Wuxian followed suit. "Wei Wuxian of Yunmeng."

Lan Xichen returned the courtesy, while Nie Huaisang shrank behind them, his voice smaller than a mosquito's buzz: "Xichen-gege..."

Lan Xichen chuckled softly. "Huaisang. I came from Qinghe not long ago, and your brother made a point to ask about your studies. Well? Do you think you'll pass this year?"

"I... I think so..." Nie Huaisang whimpered, looking like a frosted, wilted melon as he shot a pathetic, pleading look at Wei Wuxian.

Wei Wuxian chimed in with an easy grin. "Ze-wu-jun, are you heading out on business?"

"An exorcism," Lan Xichen replied. "Waterborne ghouls. We're short on hands, so I came back to fetch Wangji."

Lan Wangji’s voice was pure frost: "Brother, there is no need to linger on small talk. Time is of the essence; let us depart."

Wei Wuxian perked up instantly. "Wait, hold on! Catching water ghouls? That's our bread and butter! Ze-wu-jun, take us along, what do you say?"

Lan Xichen simply offered a mild, amused smile, while Lan Wangji shut it down flat. "Against protocol."

"What protocol?" Wei Wuxian countered. "In Yunmeng, we wrangle water ghouls practically every day. Besides, lectures are canceled anyway!"

Yunmeng was a land of sprawling lakes and endless marshes, swimming with aquatic fiends; it was home turf for the Jiang disciples. Eager to scrub away the embarrassment their clan had suffered in the Cloud Recesses over the past few days, Jiang Cheng backed him up. "He's right, Ze-wu-jun. We can pull our weight."

"Unnecessary," Lan Wangji began coldly. "The Gusu Lan Sect has plenty of—"

"Sounds splendid," Lan Xichen cut in smoothly, his smile deepening. "We would be glad for the help. Go get your gear and we'll set off together. Huaisang, will you be joining?"

Nie Huaisang desperately wanted to tag along for the spectacle, but the mere mention of his terrifying older brother had scared the mischief out of him. He wasn't about to risk it. "N-no, I'll pass! I'm heading back to hit the books..." Anything to make a show of diligence so Lan Xichen might put in a good word for him back home. Taking their cue, Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng hurried off to fetch their swords.

Watching their retreating backs, Lan Wangji’s brow furrowed in genuine disbelief. "Brother, why bring them? Night-hunts are not for frivolous play."

"Sect Leader Jiang's head disciple and only son have sterling reputations back in Yunmeng," Lan Xichen reasoned gently. "They may surprise you."

Lan Wangji remained tight-lipped, his stone-cold face screaming silent, vehement disagreement.

Lan Xichen added, "Besides... didn't you want him to come along?"

Lan Wangji froze.

Lan Xichen smiled warmly. "From the look on your face, it seemed you wished for Sect Leader Jiang's head disciple to join us. That is why I agreed."

The air outside the Elegant Room turned to solid ice.

After a suffocating silence, Lan Wangji squeezed out four strained syllables: "...Not in the slightest."

Before he could dig his heels in any further, Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng sprinted back with their swords strapped tight. Lan Wangji clamped his jaw shut, leaving the party no choice but to mount their flying swords and take to the skies.

The aquatic menace had taken root in Caiyi Town, nestled roughly twenty li outside the Cloud Recesses.

Caiyi was a maze of intersecting waterways; it was hard to tell whether the city was woven from canals, or if the whitewashed houses with gray-tiled roofs were just clinging to the edges of a watery spiderweb. The waterways were crammed with boats, wicker baskets, and bustling locals. Fruit, vegetables, bamboo carvings, pastries, and dyed silk fabrics were traded straight off the water.

Down in the Jiangnan region, even the local dialect sounded gentle, rolling off the tongue with a sweet, musical lilt. When two skiffs bumped bows and sent a couple of rice wine jars splashing into the canal, the boatmen's bickering sounded less like a brawl and more like chirping songbirds. Yunmeng had plenty of water, but nothing like this picturesque floating town. Finding it fascinating, Wei Wuxian shelled out some coins for two jars of sweet rice wine, tossing one to Jiang Cheng. "People from Gusu talk so sweet. If this counts as a fight here, sending them down to Yunmeng to hear our folks scream would scare them half to death... Lan Zhan, what's with that look? I didn't leave you out to be stingy; your clan isn't allowed to drink, remember?"

They didn't linger in the markets, chartering over a dozen narrow skiffs and punting down the current toward the trouble spot. Slowly, the cluster of houses on the banks thinned out, the water growing eerily still. Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng took up individual boats, racing each other with their poles while listening to the rundown of the hauntings.

The canal emptied into a vast lake further up: Lake Biling. For decades, Caiyi Town had been peaceful, but over the past few months, boaters had been mysteriously tumbling overboard, and heavy cargo barges were vanishing into the depths without a trace. A few days ago, Lan Xichen had laid down spiritual nets across the waters, expecting to dredge up a stray ghoul or two. Instead, they reeled in over a dozen. When the bloated faces were wiped clean and shown to the surrounding towns, not a single soul recognized the victims. Worse, when they cast the nets again yesterday, another fresh batch surfaced.

Wei Wuxian stroked his chin. "It doesn't make sense for them to be drownings from upstream washed down by the current. Water ghouls are territorial creatures—they stay bound to the exact stretch of water where they died. They rarely leave."

Lan Xichen nodded. "Precisely. Which is why this feels far from ordinary, and why I brought Wangji along for reinforcement."

Wei Wuxian asked, "Ze-wu-jun, water ghouls are cunning beasts. If we just punt along blindly and they decide to hunker down on the lakebed, how long are we supposed to scour the water? What happens if they never show?"

Lan Wangji’s voice was flat: "We search until they are found. It is our duty."

"And we're just scooping them with nets?"

"We are," Lan Xichen replied. "Does the Yunmeng Jiang Sect employ a different method?"

Wei Wuxian flashed a private, wicked grin without answering. Sure, the Jiang Clan used nets too, but blessed with freakish swimming skills, Wei Wuxian usually just dove headfirst into the murky depths and hauled the ghouls out by their hair. Naturally, that reckless stunt was entirely too unhinged to pull in front of the Lan family; if old man Lan Qiren caught wind of it, he’d be strapped down for another hundred strokes of the discipline paddle.

Changing the subject, Wei Wuxian mused, "If only we had some kind of bait that lured water ghouls straight to us. Or maybe a magical compass that pointed out their exact coordinates."

Jiang Cheng scoffed. "Keep your eyes on the water and do your job. Stop living in dreamland."

"Hey, riding flying swords used to be a pipe dream too, didn't it?" Wei Wuxian quipped.

Glancing down, his gaze drifted across the hull of Lan Wangji’s boat just ahead. A sudden realization clicked, and he barked, "Lan Zhan, heads up!"

Lan Wangji had been on high alert, his eyes snapping toward the shout on instinct—only to see Wei Wuxian sweep his bamboo pole through the water, scooping a massive, soaking wave straight toward his face!

Toe tapping the deck, Lan Wangji took to the air like a crane, landing lightly on an adjacent boat and dodging the spray entirely. Furious that the delinquent had used a night-hunt as an excuse to play pranks, he spat out, "Absurd!"

Without missing a beat, Wei Wuxian slammed his heel down against the edge of the abandoned skiff, hooking the tip of his bamboo pole beneath the gunwale to flip the vessel completely upside down.

Clinging fast to the slimy wooden planks of the hull were three bloated, corpse-white water ghouls!

The nearby disciples lunged forward, swiftly pinning the thrashing creatures with spiritual bindings. Lan Xichen’s eyes sparkled with genuine delight. "Young Master Wei, however did you realize they were lurking beneath?"

Wei Wuxian knocked his pole against his own deck with a grin. "Child's play! The water displacement was off. Wangji-xiong was the only one standing aboard, yet his boat was sinking deeper than skiffs carrying two grown men. Something had to be weighing down the keel."

Lan Xichen gave an approving nod. "Seasoned instincts indeed."

With a lazy flick of his pole, Wei Wuxian propelled his skiff forward until he was cruising side-by-side with Lan Wangji. "Lan Zhan, I wasn't splashing you on purpose, honest! Water ghouls are crafty devils—if I had shouted it out, they would've scattered into the deep. Come on, don't give me the silent treatment. Look at me, Second Young Master Lan!"

Lan Wangji deigned to cast a sideways glance, his tone heavy with suspicion: "Why did you come along?"

Wei Wuxian offered an impossibly earnest, wide-eyed look. "To apologize, of course! Last night was completely my fault. I was wrong."

A dark cloud visibly drifted across Lan Wangji’s brow, clearly not having forgotten how Wei Wuxian had tried to 'apologize' in the Library Pavilion.

Feigning total innocence, Wei Wuxian teased, "Why the long face? Don't worry, I really came to help today."

Jiang Cheng couldn't stomach the flirting a second longer. "If you're here to help, shut your mouth and get over here!"

A disciple suddenly shouted from the lead boat: "The nets are pulling!"

Sure enough, the thick cords jerked violently against the surface. Wei Wuxian perked up, eyes flashing. "Here they come!"

Masses of slick, raven-black hair erupted through the ripples around a dozen skiffs like drifting silk. A forest of pale, waterlogged hands clamped onto the wooden gunwales! Lan Wangji didn't hesitate; Bichen slid from its scabbard in a reverse grip, cleaving a clean dozen wrists off the port side, leaving severed, dead-white fingers still embedded in the wood. Just as he pivoted to clear the starboard, a streak of crimson spiritual light tore through the air—and Wei Wuxian was already clicking his blade back into its sheath.

The turmoil under the surface died down, the nets going slack once more.

Wei Wuxian’s strike had been blindingly fast, but Lan Wangji’s sharp eyes had caught the undeniable brilliance of a high-grade spiritual sword. Standing tall, he asked with grave solemnity: "What is the name of this blade?"

Wei Wuxian blinked. "Suibian."*

Lan Wangji stared at him. Assuming the noise had muffled his voice, Wei Wuxian repeated it, louder: "Suibian!"

Lan Wangji’s brow knit into a severe frown, his voice tight with disapproval. "A spiritual blade possesses a soul of its own. To refer to it so carelessly is a disgrace."

Wei Wuxian sighed, shaking his head. "Loosen up, will you? I'm not telling you to call it 'whatever,' the sword’s actual name is Suibian! Look, see for yourself." He tilted the hilt out, pointing out the ancient seal script carved into the fittings. Clear as day, the characters read: Sui Bian.

Lan Wangji was struck completely speechless.

Wei Wuxian chuckled warmly, offering a helpful explanation: "No need to look so dumbfounded, I know what you're thinking. Everyone asks if there's some profound, poetic lore behind it. Honestly? There isn't. When Uncle Jiang gifted me the sword, he asked what I wanted to name it. I brainstormed over twenty grand, poetic titles, but none of them felt right. Finally, I just threw my hands up and said, 'Whatever!' Who knew that when the smith pulled the finished steel from the forge, those were the exact two characters carved into the hilt! Uncle Jiang shrugged and said, 'If that's your wish, Suibian it is.' Personally, I think it's a pretty sweet name, don't you?"

After a painful silence, Lan Wangji squeezed out a single word from behind gritted teeth: "...Ludicrous!"

Wei Wuxian casually rested the sheathed blade across his shoulder, grinning wickedly. "You're no fun at all, Lan Zhan. It's a hilarious name! It baits serious, stuck-up guys like you every single time, haha!"

Right as the laughter left his lips, an enormous, serpentine shadow darted across the dark emerald depths of the lake, circling their tiny fleet.

Jiang Cheng, having just cleared the stragglers on his flank, caught the motion from the corner of his eye and barked: "Heads up—it's back!"

*A/N: In Chinese, 随便 (suíbiàn) literally translates to "whatever," "as you please," or "casually." When Uncle Jiang asked a young Wei Wuxian what he wanted to name his sword, Wei Wuxian flippantly replied "Suibian" (meaning "whatever you want"), and the swordsmith took it literally, engraving "Whatever" onto the steel.
